newsitem.title: USA: Wash. Grand Coulee dam flows cut on flood concerns.
newsitem.headline: Wash. Grand Coulee dam flows cut on flood concerns.

text.p: Flows out of Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia River in Washington state are being capped near 140,000 cubic feet per second (cfs) amid concerns about potential downstream flooding, a spokesman for the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, the dam's operator, said Wednesday.

But discharge can still be shaped to maximize generation during peak demand hours, and flow volumes will vary depending on systemwide river conditions, noted a source at the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA).
"There is no need to run flat out of Coulee. The discharge has to be flat out of Bonneville (Dam), but that's a day later," he explained.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers requested limits at Grand Coulee so that discharge from Bonneville Dam, the Columbia's furthest downstream project, can be kept at 440,000 cfs.
Powerhouse hydraulic capacity for Grand Coulee is listed at 280,000 cfs, while generating capacity is listed at 6,150 megawatts (MW).
But one of the dam's 600 MW turbines has been off-line for maintenance since February and is scheduled to be out of service until early August.
Inflows to the dam are projected at 160,000 to 165,000 cfs over the next several days, compared with recent rates of 110,000 to 120,000 cfs.
Until Tuesday, Grand Coulee was being operated to draw down reservoir levels in anticipation of the heavy inflows, but this drafting is now on hold, the Corps of Engineers said.
